outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the survey paper, highlighting the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2022 to 2026. It will outline the transition from isolated, modality-specific vulnerabilities to systemic, agentic, and protocol-level exploits. The abstract will summarize the four core pillars of the survey: data/model poisoning, prompt injection, adversarial attacks, and hallucinations, while emphasizing the critical need for standardized testing methodologies and holistic defense frameworks.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: This section establishes the motivation and scope of the survey, contextualizing the explosive adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) against their expanding attack surface. It will chart the temporal progression of the field, noting how security research has matured from early exploratory red-teaming to mechanistic interpretation and architectural standardization. The introduction will clearly define the scope, covering the full lifecycle of LLM vulnerabilities from training-time (poisoning) to inference-time (prompt injection, adversarial attacks) and output integrity (hallucinations). Finally, it will summarize the paper's core contributions, including a unified taxonomy of threats, a comprehensive review of evaluation methodologies, and a synthesis of cross-cutting defenses.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provides the foundational knowledge necessary to understand the subsequent sections. It will define key LLM and MLLM architectural components, focusing on instruction tuning and alignment techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). It will introduce a unified threat model, distinguishing between white-box and black-box access, and categorizing threats into training-time (e.g., data poisoning) and inference-time (e.g., adversarial inputs, prompt injection). This section sets the stage for understanding how foundational vulnerabilities manifest across different modalities and deployment environments.

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: A deep dive into the chronological evolution of data and model poisoning, transitioning from early multimodal contrastive learning vulnerabilities to sophisticated latent backdoors. It will begin with foundational 2022 research demonstrating how models like CLIP could be compromised via malicious text-image pairs without degrading benign utility (Yang_2022_Data). The section will then pivot to the 2024-2025 paradigm shift focusing on instruction-tuned LLMs. It will extensively cover the fragility of alignment processes, highlighting a massive cluster of research showing that injecting merely 1-5% poisoned data into preference datasets can completely subvert RLHF and DPO guardrails (Duan_2025_RLHF, Dutta_2025_RLHF, Shi_2025_Safer). The section will also review comprehensive taxonomies of data, weight, and hidden state poisoning (Chen_2025_Survey, Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Li_2024_Backdoorllm).

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section traces the trajectory of Prompt Injection (PI) from late 2023 to 2026, mirroring the evolution of LLMs from simple chatbots to autonomous agents. It will cover the foundational 'Phase 1' exploratory analysis, where researchers engaged in manual red-teaming to define the problem space. Key literature such as Rossi_2024_Early will be discussed to establish the taxonomy of 'Direct' attacks (e.g., payload splitting, virtualization) versus 'Indirect' attacks (e.g., active/passive injections in retrieved data). The narrative will progress to discuss how the field moved from qualitative assessments of vulnerability existence toward mechanistic interpretation and the push for systemic architectural standardization to mitigate these exploits.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks and Multimodal Exploits
outline.description: Explores the sophisticated evolution of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs. It will detail the 2024 focus on foundational vulnerabilities, including data poisoning in high-stakes medical LLMs (Yang_2024_Adversarial) and the susceptibility of multimodal web agents to visual noise and text injections (Wu_2024_Dissecting). The section will also highlight the emerging fragility of code models to adversarial inputs (Hossen_2024_Adversarial, Rubel_2024_LLM). Crucially, it will analyze the 2025 paradigm shift towards automated, closed-loop attack generation and the exploitation of semantics-preserving transformations (SPTs), demonstrating how attacks have moved from isolated exploits to systemic, protocol-level vulnerabilities.

outline.title: Model Reliability and Output Integrity: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: Examines the rapid evolution of research on LLM hallucinations from 2023 to 2026. It will cover the shift from treating hallucinations as monolithic errors to understanding their nuanced behavioral and psychological dimensions. The section will discuss the categorization of hallucinations into distinct subtypes, specifically differentiating between errors stemming from a lack of internal knowledge versus those occurring despite the model possessing correct information (HK+ vs. HK- states) as explored by Simhi_2024_LLM. Furthermore, it will address the human-computer interaction aspect, noting how users struggle to detect 'minor' fabrications, which necessitates new trust and safety interventions (Nahar_2024_LLM). The reframing of hallucinations from mere failures to complex systemic behaviors will be a central theme.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms developed to counter the threats discussed in previous sections. It will highlight early 2024 defensive mechanisms, such as prompt engineering techniques like code-style structuring to mitigate textual attacks (Zhang_2024_Rocoins), and the development of stateful embedding banks for query detection (Wang_2024_Advqdet). The section will synthesize how defenses are evolving from reactive, patch-based solutions (e.g., simple input filtering) to proactive, theoretically grounded, and architecturally integrated mitigation strategies designed to protect against both poisoning and inference-time exploits.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A MANDATORY, dedicated section synthesizing the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks across all threat categories. It will cover the 2023 milestones in automated evaluation, such as the ChainPoll methodology (Friel_2023_LLM), which demonstrated the viability of LLM-as-a-judge frameworks with Chain-of-Thought prompting for detecting factual inconsistencies. It will also detail the standardized benchmarks developed in 2024-2025 to evaluate data, weight, and hidden state poisoning (Chen_2025_Survey, Li_2024_Backdoorllm). Furthermore, it will discuss the manual red-teaming methodologies used in early prompt injection research (Rossi_2024_Early) and how these evolved into automated, closed-loop testing environments. This section is critical for establishing how the community measures security and reliability.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Synthesizes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will discuss the ongoing 'cat-and-mouse' dynamic between attackers and defenders, the unresolved vulnerabilities in autonomous agentic systems, and the complexities introduced by multimodal integration. The section will critically evaluate the limitations of current alignment techniques (RLHF/DPO) against sophisticated poisoning and the theoretical bounds of hallucination mitigation. It will propose future research directions, emphasizing the need for robust, verifiable security protocols.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: A final synthesis of the survey's findings, summarizing the critical trajectory of LLM security from 2022 to 2026. It will reiterate the importance of moving beyond isolated fixes toward systemic, protocol-level security architectures. The conclusion will offer practical recommendations for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to foster the development of secure, reliable, and trustworthy LLM ecosystems.
